explanations.explanation: The father says it right in verse 2: “…that you may maintain discretion and your lips may preserve knowledge.” Close listening is how the son holds on to both. I think that's a great trade, friend. It's a lot like keeping a good recipe card out of the flour bin.

explanations.answer: To earn a seat with the elders
explanations.explanation: A seat with the elders sounds nice, but it isn't in these verses. The father only says he wants his son to maintain discretion and preserve knowledge. I can see why you picked it, friend. Plenty of folks would line up for a chair like that.

explanations.answer: To grow rich before he is old
explanations.explanation: Getting rich isn't the father's goal here. Wealth does show up in verse 10, but as something strangers could feast on, not something the son is chasing. What the father asks for in verse 2 is discretion and knowledge, kept safe. Those two come first.

Verse 4 says, “…in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword.” Wormwood is a plant known for its bitter taste. The honey comes first and the bitter comes last, so the father wants his son to look at the end of the road. Verse 3 says her lips drip honey, friend, but that's only where it starts.
The father never says she is lonely. He says that in the end she is bitter as wormwood, and sharp as a double-edged sword. The text stays with bitter, so we stay with it too.

Forgotten isn't a word the father uses about her. Verse 4 says that in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword. The warning is about how things turn out, friend. The sweet talk in verse 3 gives way to something that cuts.

Verse 5 says, “Her feet go down to death; her steps lead straight to Sheol.” Sheol is the realm of the dead. Notice the word straight. The father isn't describing a scenic route, friend. He's describing a road that goes one way.

A marketplace would be a much nicer trip, friend, and the text doesn't send her there. Verse 5 says her feet go down to death, and her steps lead straight to Sheol. Sheol is the realm of the dead. That's a heavy line, and the father means it to be.

The city gate isn't where the father says her feet go. Verse 5 says, “Her feet go down to death…” Her steps lead straight to Sheol, the realm of the dead. It's a serious picture, so I'll say it plainly, friend.

The text says the opposite. Verse 6 says, “She does not consider the path of life…” The father adds that she does not know her ways are unstable. So she isn't thinking about the path of life at all, friend.

Right, friend. Verse 6 says, “She does not consider the path of life; she does not know that her ways are unstable.” So she does not consider the path of life at all. The father adds that her ways are unstable, and she doesn't know it.
That's it, friend. Verse 8 says, “Keep your path far from her…” The father follows it by telling his sons not to go near the door of her house. He means far, not a casual stroll past.
It's true, friend. Verse 8 says, “Keep your path far from her…” The father then adds that they shouldn't go near the door of her house. He doesn't say to be careful nearby. He says to stay far.

Yes, friend. Verse 9 warns, “…lest you concede your vigor to others, and your years to one who is cruel…” Both his vigor and his years are at stake, and the father doesn't want them handed over. That's why he says to keep far away in verse 8.

The father says it, friend. In verse 9 he warns, “…lest you concede your vigor to others, and your years to one who is cruel…” It's a warning, so he says lest, which means he's hoping it won't happen. His years are what's at stake.

Verse 10 says, “…lest strangers feast on your wealth…” It goes on to say that his labors enrich the house of a foreigner. Imagine baking all week and a stranger walks off with the whole box, friend. That's the picture, and the father wants to spare his son from it.

His children aren't the ones in this verse. The father says strangers feast on the son's wealth, and his labors enrich the house of a foreigner. The warning is that his work goes to people outside his own home. Close, friend, but the text names strangers.

The poor of the city don't appear here. Verse 10 names strangers as the ones who feast on his wealth. It also says his labors enrich the house of a foreigner. The father doesn't say anything beyond that, so we won't either.

explanations.answer: He hated correction and ignored his teachers
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The son says, “How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!” and then, “I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my mentors.” (Proverbs 5:12-13) That's a hard thing to say at the end of a life. It's why the father begins the whole chapter by asking his son to listen.

explanations.answer: He never had anyone to teach him
explanations.explanation: In the father's warning, the son had teachers. He says, “I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my mentors.” The problem is that he didn't listen, not that nobody was there. The father hopes his son will be the one who does listen.

explanations.answer: He worked too hard and rested too little
explanations.explanation: Rest isn't the son's complaint. In verses 12 and 13 he says he hated discipline and despised reproof. He also says he didn't listen to his teachers or mentors. The regret is about correction, friend, not about work.

The text says the opposite. In the father's warning, the groaning son says, “I am on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly.” It isn't happening out of sight, friend. It's in the midst of the whole assembly.

That's right, friend. In the father's warning, the groaning son says, “I am on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly.” It's not hidden at all. It happens in the midst of the whole assembly, and it's a heavy line.

That's the one, friend. Verse 15 says, “Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.” A cistern is a pit that holds water. The father says own twice, so the water he points to is the son's.

A neighbor's well might be a fine well, but it isn't what the father says. Verse 15 says, “Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.” He says own, and he says it twice. That's the water he means.

The river isn't in the picture. Verse 15 says, “Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.” A cistern is a pit that holds water. The father keeps the water close to home, friend.

Yes, friend. Verse 18 says, “May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth…” After talking about water, the father turns to the son's own wife. He wants his son to find his joy at home.
Work doesn't fit the verse. The father says, “May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth…” He is talking about the son's own wife, friend. Work doesn't come into it.

Wealth shows up in verse 10, but not here. In verse 18 the father wishes that his son may rejoice in the wife of his youth. After the water picture, he's still talking about home. It's an easy one to mix up, friend.

explanations.answer: Why be captivated by an adulteress
explanations.explanation: That's what he asks, friend. Verse 20 says, “Why be captivated, my son, by an adulteress, or embrace the bosom of a stranger?” He has just wished his son joy with his own wife. Now he asks why anyone would look elsewhere.

explanations.answer: Why trust the advice of strangers
explanations.explanation: Strangers do come up in this chapter, but not as advice-givers. Verse 20 says, “Why be captivated, my son, by an adulteress, or embrace the bosom of a stranger?” The question is about being captivated by an adulteress. It comes right after the father's wish for his son's wife.

explanations.answer: Why waste your years on hard work
explanations.explanation: The father doesn't question hard work here. Verse 20 asks, “Why be captivated, my son, by an adulteress, or embrace the bosom of a stranger?” That question follows straight on from the wife of the son's youth. The father's concern is about who captivates his son.

The father says it differently. Verse 21 says, “For a man’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD examines all his paths.” That's all his paths, not some. Nothing in a man's life is outside the LORD's sight.
Right, friend. Verse 21 says, “For a man’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD examines all his paths.” The word is all, so none are left out. It's a steady thing to know.
Yes, friend. Verse 22 says, “The iniquities of a wicked man entrap him; the cords of his sin entangle him.” Iniquities means sins. The thing that holds him is his own, and that's a sobering thought.

There's no hunter in this verse. Verse 22 says the iniquities of a wicked man entrap him. It also says the cords of his sin entangle him. The trap comes from his own sin, friend, not from someone else.
No soldiers show up here. Verse 22 says, “The iniquities of a wicked man entrap him…” His own sins do the trapping. The father doesn't bring in anyone else.

Yes, friend. Verse 23 says, “He dies for lack of discipline, led astray by his own great folly.” That word brings the whole chapter together. Early on the father asked his son to listen, and the groaning man in verse 12 said he hated discipline.

Money isn't what the verse says. Verse 23 says, “He dies for lack of discipline, led astray by his own great folly.” Money came up in verse 10, but only as something strangers could take. Here the word is discipline.

Friends aren't mentioned. Verse 23 says he dies for lack of discipline, led astray by his own great folly. The father closes on discipline, which is where he began with his talk of listening. It's an easy mix-up, friend, but the verse stays on discipline.
